# Appetite and weight regulation

> *Hunger, fullness and body weight are regulated by signals from the gut and fat tissue acting on
> circuits in the brain, and these signals respond far more strongly to weight loss than to weight gain.
> We cover how hunger and fullness are controlled, what makes a meal filling, the reward system behind
> eating for pleasure, and why lost weight is often regained, which is the basis for talking about weight
> without blame.*

::: {.callout-note}
## Learning objectives
- Explain how hunger-promoting (AgRP/NPY) and satiety-promoting (POMC/CART) neurons in the arcuate
  nucleus are balanced at MC4R to set hunger.
- Distinguish leptin's long-term signal of fat stores from the short-term gut-hormone signals of each
  meal, and explain why leptin does not treat common obesity.
- Distinguish hunger, satiation and satiety, and explain how protein, energy density, fibre, food form
  and eating rate change fullness for the same calories.
- Explain how the reward system (wanting, liking and food cues) can override fullness.
- Explain why weight lost by dieting tends to return, and how short sleep (and, plausibly, chronic
  stress) biases appetite toward hunger.
- Explain why weight returns when a GLP-1 receptor agonist is stopped, and use the biology of
  body-weight regulation to discuss weight without blame.
:::

## Appetite and weight regulation at a glance {#sec-overview}

Energy balance can be written as arithmetic, calories in minus calories out (see the
[*Energy balance*](energy-balance.qmd#sec-overview) chapter). That arithmetic holds, but its terms are not freely
chosen. Appetite is a **controlled variable**: an integrated system of hormones and brain circuits
regulates it, as other homeostatic systems regulate blood glucose and body temperature. Appetite is not
simply a matter of conscious choice.

The system uses two kinds of signal. The long-term signal is leptin, released by fat in proportion to
fat mass, which signals to the brain how large the fat stores are over days and weeks. The short-term
signals are gut hormones that rise and fall across a single meal and govern when a meal starts and
when it ends. Both act on circuits in the hypothalamus that set hunger. The brain's **reward system**,
which drives eating because food is pleasurable and available, can override fullness when such food
is abundant. Body weight itself is regulated, and the responses that oppose weight loss
are far stronger than those that oppose weight gain.

Appetite is therefore a regulated biological drive, not a matter of willpower. The same physiology
explains cravings, regain after a diet and why weight is so hard to lose. A few modifiable factors
(protein and fibre, portion sizes and drink choices, sleep and stress) are more useful than simply advising patients to eat less. This physiology is the basis for managing weight without blame, and the reason "eat less, move more"
is true but insufficient.

## How hunger and fullness are controlled {#sec-control}

Hunger depends on the balance between two opposing sets of hypothalamic neurons, and two kinds of signal shift that balance: long-term signals of fat stores, chiefly leptin, and gut hormones, which signal each meal as it is eaten.

### Hypothalamic control of appetite {#sec-thermostat}

A cluster of neurons in the hypothalamus sets hunger. Its sensing hub is the **arcuate nucleus**, which
lies beside a gap in the blood–brain barrier and so can sense circulating hunger and fullness
hormones. The arcuate nucleus contains two opposing populations of neurons:

AgRP/NPY neurons
: Neurons that release agouti-related peptide (AgRP) and neuropeptide Y (NPY). They are orexigenic
  (hunger-promoting): activating them in a well-fed mouse makes it eat voraciously within minutes
  [@aponte2011agrp].

POMC/CART neurons
: Neurons that make pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC) and cocaine- and amphetamine-regulated transcript
  (CART). They are anorexigenic (appetite-suppressing). POMC is cleaved to form a smaller peptide, α-MSH
  (α-melanocyte-stimulating hormone), that signals "stop eating".

The two populations oppose each other directly: the AgRP/NPY neurons inhibit the POMC/CART neurons.
Both converge on a single receptor, the **melanocortin-4 receptor (MC4R)**. α-MSH activates MC4R to
reduce eating, while AgRP blocks the same receptor to increase eating. MC4R is therefore where the two
opposing drives are summed [@andermann2017wiring]. The peripheral hormones (leptin, insulin, ghrelin
and PYY) all act by shifting this balance one way or the other.

The interactive below, the appetite thermostat, draws the AgRP/NPY neurons as an accelerator and the
POMC/CART neurons as a brake. Step it through its four states (fasted, just ate, after weight loss and
on a GLP-1 drug) and watch the balance between them shift. (The last two states are explained in
[Body-weight regulation and weight regain](#sec-defended).)

<div data-island="appetite-thermostat" data-src="/diagrams/appetite-thermostat.yml"></div>

::: {.callout-important}
## MC4R deficiency: the same circuit in humans
MC4R mutations are the commonest single-gene cause of severe obesity, found in about 6% of people
with severe childhood-onset obesity, and the more a mutation damages the receptor, the hungrier and
heavier the person [@farooqi2003mc4r]. When the receptor cannot respond to α-MSH, the satiety signal
cannot act and appetite remains persistently high. Hunger is, in this sense, set by biology.
:::

### Leptin: long-term signalling of fat stores {#sec-leptin}

Physiologists long suspected that fat tissue sends the brain a signal of how much is stored. In 1994,
cloning the gene mutated in a grossly obese mouse revealed it: leptin, a hormone made by fat in
proportion to fat mass [@zhang1994leptin]. More fat means more leptin and, normally, less hunger.
Leptin acts directly on the arcuate nucleus: it activates the POMC/CART neurons and inhibits the
AgRP/NPY neurons. Because its level tracks fat mass, leptin is the brain's long-term signal of fat
stores. Insulin is a second, weaker long-term signal to the same neurons. (Leptin also appears in the *Energy balance* chapter, and both leptin and the metabolic actions of insulin in the [*Integrative metabolism*](integrative-metabolism.qmd#sec-fed) chapter.)

Children with **congenital leptin deficiency**, who are born unable to make leptin, show that leptin is
necessary for normal human appetite. They have extreme, early-onset obesity with relentless hunger
[@montague1997congenital]. In the first children treated, daily leptin injections reversed this:
appetite fell sharply and they lost weight that was almost entirely fat, with the benefit sustained for
years [@farooqi1999leptintherapy; @farooqi2002leptin].

::: {.callout-important}
## Why doesn't leptin treat common obesity?
Because leptin suppresses appetite, it looked like a possible treatment for obesity in general. People
with common obesity, however, already have high leptin, since more fat makes more of it, and the brain
has stopped responding to it: **leptin resistance**.
Recombinant leptin given to people with common obesity produced only modest, highly variable weight
loss, far less than in the leptin-deficient children [@heymsfield1999recombinant].
Leptin therapy therefore works for the rare deficiency and not for common obesity.

The current view is that leptin is less an "anti-fat hormone" than a starvation signal: a fall in
leptin drives hunger and refeeding, while a rise has comparatively little effect, an asymmetry that
underlies weight regain [@flier2024leptin30] (see
[Body-weight regulation and weight regain](#sec-defended)).
:::

### Gut hormones: short-term hunger and satiety signals {#sec-gut-peptides}

While leptin tracks fat stores over weeks, gut hormones signal to the brain about each meal as it is
eaten. Two of these gut hormones appear in the
[*Digestion and absorption*](digestion-absorption.qmd) chapter for
their actions on the gut: CCK, which makes the gallbladder contract, and GLP-1 (glucagon-like
peptide-1), an incretin that helps trigger insulin release. For appetite, what matters is what the gut
hormones signal to the brain.

**Ghrelin**, made by the stomach, is the only gut hormone that drives hunger. It rises before meals
and falls after eating, which is why it is called the hunger hormone [@kojima1999ghrelin;
@cummings2001preprandial]. Part of the pre-meal rise appears to be learned: in rats fed on a fixed
schedule, ghrelin climbs in anticipation of the usual meal time [@drazen2006fixedmeal], so hunger may
partly follow the clock (and the smell of the hawker centre) as well as an empty stomach. In a small
human study, protein suppressed ghrelin the most overall, while after carbohydrate it rebounded above
its pre-meal level [@fosterschubert2008ghrelin], which may be part of why protein is so filling.

The **satiety peptides**, hormones that signal fullness, are released as food arrives, roughly in
proportion to the calories eaten. They differ in where they are made and in how they curb eating:

| Satiety peptide | Where it is made | Effect on eating |
|---|---|---|
| CCK | Duodenum, triggered by fat and protein | A short, meal-ending signal; the first satiety hormone identified [@gibbs1973cck] |
| GLP-1 and PYY (peptide YY) | Cells lower down the small intestine | PYY at normal post-meal levels cuts food intake by about a third [@batterham2002pyy]; GLP-1 is the hormone the newer weight-loss drugs mimic (see [Obesity and GLP-1 receptor agonists](#sec-obesity)) |
| Amylin | Pancreas, released with insulin at each meal | Reduces meal size and slows the stomach [@lutz2010amylin; @mietlickibaase2016amylin] |

These signals reach the brain mostly along the vagus nerve, through a relay in the brainstem (the
nucleus of the solitary tract, NTS) and up to the hypothalamus, a direct neural pathway for fullness.
A second signal is purely mechanical: stretch of the stomach wall produces fullness that depends on
volume, not calories. That is why a big bowl of soup or salad feels filling for very few calories.

::: {.callout-note}
## The ileal brake and the microbiome
When food reaches the far end of the small intestine, the GLP-1/PYY cells there both slow the
stomach and signal fullness, a feedback loop called the **ileal brake** that paces digestion and
appetite together. Short-chain fatty acids, which gut bacteria make from fibre (see [*The
gut microbiome*](gut-microbiome.qmd#sec-scfa) chapter), stimulate these same GLP-1/PYY cells, so
fibre fermented in the colon also promotes satiety.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: many hormones signal hunger and fullness, yet a fault in one receptor, MC4R, causes relentless hunger. Why does one receptor matter so much?
The hunger-promoting AgRP/NPY neurons and the appetite-suppressing POMC/CART neurons converge on MC4R:
α-MSH from the POMC/CART neurons activates it to reduce eating, and AgRP blocks it to increase eating.
MC4R is therefore where the two drives are summed, and the peripheral hormones act by shifting that
balance. When the receptor is damaged, the α-MSH satiety signal cannot act there, so appetite stays
relentlessly high.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: people with common obesity have high leptin. Why does giving them more leptin do so little?
More fat makes more leptin, and in common obesity the brain has stopped responding to it (leptin
resistance), so recombinant leptin produced only modest, variable weight loss. On the current
view, leptin acts mainly as a starvation signal: a fall drives hunger and refeeding, while a rise
has little effect. Leptin therapy works for the rare congenital leptin deficiency, not for common
obesity.
:::

## What makes a meal filling {#sec-satiety}

Three everyday words describe different parts of the fullness cycle [@benelam2009satiation], and they
are easily confused:

Hunger
: The drive that starts a meal.

Satiation
: The fullness that builds during a meal and ends it; it sets meal size.

Satiety
: The fullness after a meal that delays the next one; it sets how long until hunger returns.

The signals behind satiation and satiety unfold over time in a **satiety cascade**
[@blundell2010appetite]:

::: {.flow}
[The satiety cascade]{.tree-title}

1. Sensory: taste and pleasure
2. Cognitive: how much has been eaten
3. Gut signals: stretch, CCK, then GLP-1 and PYY
4. Absorbed nutrients
:::

What and how people eat changes fullness for the same calories, through five factors:

| Factor | Why it works | Practical version |
|---|---|---|
| Protein | Most satiating macronutrient; strongly raises PYY and acutely suppresses ghrelin [@batterham2006pyyprotein; @fosterschubert2008ghrelin] | Build meals around a protein source |
| Energy density | People eat a fairly constant volume; water and fibre in the food lower calories per bite | Bulk meals with vegetables |
| Viscous fibre | Thickens or gels in the stomach, so the same volume feels fuller [@hoad2004gelation]; may slow stomach emptying [@georgjensen2012alginate] | Oats, legumes, wholegrains |
| Solid over liquid | Liquid calories give weak fullness and little compensation | Eat whole fruit rather than drinking juice |
| Eating rate | Slower eating lowers intake, probably because fullness signals lag behind the meal [@robinson2014eatingrate] | Slow down |

Two studies quantify these effects. The first concerned protein: when 19 volunteers' protein intake was raised from
15% to 30% of energy (carbohydrate held constant), they spontaneously ate about 440 kcal/day less and lost about 4.9 kg over
12 weeks, with no instruction to eat less [@weigle2005highprotein]. Liquid calories, by contrast, are
poorly compensated for. When 450 kcal/day was eaten as jelly beans, it was fully compensated for (no
weight gain), but the same 450 kcal drunk as soft drink was not, and caused weight gain
[@dimeglio2000liquidsolid].

::: {.callout-tip}
## 🍜 Eating for fullness in Singapore
A hawker plate of *char kway teow* or chicken rice is energy-dense and low in fibre, and it is often
washed down with a sweet drink, a combination that empties the stomach fast and brings hunger back
soon. Swaps that keep people full for longer use the factors above:

- Add a protein (fish, tofu, egg, *tau kwa*).
- Ask for more vegetables.
- Choose brown or mixed rice.
- Take the drink *kosong* (no sugar), or plain water.
- Slow down.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## 🍳 Healthy kitchen: add volume and eat slowly
At home the same principles apply: bulk meals with vegetables to cut energy density without cutting
volume, keep protein and fibre in every meal, and serve food that takes chewing and time over soft,
fast-to-eat food. Because fullness signals lag the meal by many minutes, slowing down is one of the
few free, evidence-backed ways to eat less without feeling deprived [@robinson2014eatingrate].
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: raising protein from 15% to 30% of energy made volunteers eat less without being told to. Why?
Protein is the most satiating macronutrient, so higher-protein meals leave people fuller for the same
calories. The volunteers were never told to eat less, so the fall of about 440 kcal/day (and about
4.9 kg over 12 weeks) came from their own fullness, not from a deliberate decision to eat less. Changing what
was eaten changed how much was eaten.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: why does eating more slowly reduce intake without leaving a person feeling deprived?
Fullness signals lag the meal by many minutes, arriving in sequence: stomach stretch, CCK, then
GLP-1 and PYY. With fast eating, more is eaten before satiation can end the meal. Eating
slowly gives the signals time to act, so the meal ends at a smaller size and the person still feels
full.
:::

## Eating for pleasure: the reward system {#sec-hedonic}

People eat when energy is low, and also when food is pleasurable and available. The reward system
drives the second kind of eating, and in a modern food environment it can override fullness
entirely. Its central distinction is between wanting a food and liking it.

::: {.callout-important}
## Is dopamine the pleasure chemical?
Because dopamine drives the pull toward rewarding food, it is often taken to be the brain's pleasure
chemical. The brain in fact separates **wanting** a food (the motivational pull, driven by dopamine)
from **liking** it (the actual pleasure, driven by separate opioid "hotspots")
[@berridge2009dissecting]. The two can come apart: a person can intensely crave a food they no
longer much enjoy. Dopamine drives the pursuit, not the pleasure, so craving is a normal feature of
a motivation system.
:::

Two everyday phenomena follow. **Hedonic hunger** is wanting food for pleasure with no energy need,
the experience of being full but still eating [@lowe2007hedonic]. **Sensory-specific satiety**
explains "always room for dessert": the pleasantness of a food falls as it is eaten, but a different
food (something sweet after a savoury meal) stays appealing [@rolls1981sensory]. The same effect is
why buffets and variety make people eat more.

**Food cues**, the sight, smell and advertising of food, also trigger the reward system, and they
can spark food-seeking even after a full meal [@volkow2017dopamine].

The foods themselves can also be built to trigger the reward system. **Ultra-processed foods** are
industrial formulations made largely from refined ingredients and additives, with little intact whole food. One measure of such foods is **hyper-palatability**: pairing fat with sugar or salt, or carbohydrate with salt, above set thresholds. By one such definition, 62% of foods in a US food database qualified [@fazzino2019hyperpalatable].

The strongest controlled evidence that ultra-processed foods drive overeating comes from a small
inpatient trial (see the *Digestion and absorption* chapter). Twenty adults on a metabolic ward ate an
ultra-processed diet and an unprocessed one for two weeks each. The diets were matched for the calories
presented, energy density, macronutrients, sugar, salt and fibre, yet people still ate about
500 kcal/day more on the ultra-processed diet [@hall2019upf]. The trial was small and short, and why
people ate more on the ultra-processed diet is still unclear. Overeating in this setting is a
normal reward system responding to an abnormal environment, not a character flaw
[@berthoud2017blaming].

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: after a large savoury dinner, a patient eats dessert although she "wasn't even hungry". Is this a failure of self-control?
No. Sensory-specific satiety lowers the pleasantness of the food being eaten while a different food,
such as something sweet after a savoury meal, stays appealing. Wanting food for pleasure with no
energy need is hedonic hunger. Both are normal responses of a reward system that can override
fullness.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: in a controlled trial, people ate about 500 kcal/day more on an ultra-processed diet than on a matched unprocessed one. What does that imply about overeating?
The diets were matched for the calories presented, macronutrients, sugar, fat, salt and fibre, so the
extra intake came from the foods, not from the eaters' character. Overeating in this setting is a
normal reward system responding to an abnormal environment.
:::

## Body-weight regulation and weight regain {#sec-defended}

Body weight is actively regulated, and the regulation is asymmetric: the responses that oppose weight
loss are strong, and those that oppose weight gain are weak. Models of this regulation should be
weighed with care. No single set point for body weight has ever been located; the current view is a
**defended range**, with a strong lower limit against starvation and a weak upper one
[@speakman2018lipostatic]. The response to weight loss, however, is not in doubt.

After substantial weight loss, three systems shift together, and all three favour regain:

- Leptin falls, and falls disproportionately low, so the hypothalamus responds as it would to
  starvation, even in a normal-weight body.
- The hunger hormones shift: ghrelin rises, the satiety peptides fall and measured hunger goes up,
  and these changes persist a full year after the weight loss [@sumithran2011hormonal].
- Energy expenditure falls more than would be predicted for the smaller body. This extra fall is adaptive
  thermogenesis, also called metabolic adaptation (see the *Energy balance* chapter), and it lowers
  the expenditure side of the energy-balance equation. A weight-reduced person spends less energy
  than someone of the same weight who was never heavier, which favours
  regain.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Does dieting permanently damage the metabolism?
The claim that "dieting permanently wrecks your metabolism" comes largely from one study. Contestants
on *The Biggest Loser* who lost about 58 kg had, six years later, resting metabolic rates about
500 kcal/day below what their body size predicted [@fothergill2016biggestloser]. The study's own
senior author later revisited the data. The contestants who kept the weight off were also those who
sustained large increases in physical activity, and under an energy-compensation model that ongoing effort, not permanent damage, lowers
resting metabolism [@hall2022biggestloser]. In ordinary dieters, metabolic adaptation is real
but modest and largely reversible, and the *Biggest Loser* cohort is an extreme outlier. Adaptation makes
weight maintenance hard; it does not make weight loss impossible or leave the metabolism "broken".
:::

### Sleep and stress: two neglected influences {#sec-sleep-stress}

Sleep and stress are two modifiable influences on appetite that the "eat less, move more" message leaves out, and both
bias the same system toward hunger.

**Short sleep increases hunger.** In a controlled experiment, two nights restricted to
4 h of sleep lowered leptin by about 18%, raised ghrelin by about 28% and raised hunger by about 24%,
especially for
calorie-dense foods [@sleepRestriction]. Pooled across trials, partial sleep loss adds on average
about 385 kcal/day of intake with no rise in energy expenditure, a clear shift toward positive energy
balance [@alkhatib2017partialsleep]. Sleep loss also weakens cortical control over eating (a
"cortical brake") and amplifies reward responses to food [@greer2013sleepdeprivation]. Meal timing
matters too: eating late, against the circadian (body) clock, raises hunger and lowers energy
expenditure even at identical calories [@vujovic2022lateeating], one reason shift work and late
suppers are metabolically taxing.

**Chronic stress nudges eating toward "comfort food".** Sustained cortisol is thought to drive a
preference for energy-dense, sugary-fatty food and to favour visceral (belly) fat [@dallman2003].
The evidence is largely animal models and human associations: people with higher long-term cortisol
do tend to carry more central fat [@jackson2017haircortisol], so the link is plausible but not
proven.

### Obesity and GLP-1 receptor agonists {#sec-obesity}

In obesity, the same regulatory system maintains an elevated weight, so the problem is not a failure
of discipline. A person with obesity is working against homeostatic signals that maintain the higher
weight: high but ineffective leptin, a hunger drive that rises as soon as weight is lost, and energy
expenditure that adapts. Obesity is increasingly understood as a condition of a dysregulated system,
not a lifestyle choice. A 2025 commission distinguishes two forms: *clinical* obesity, in which excess fat
already impairs how organs or the whole person function, is a chronic disease, whereas *preclinical*
obesity, with function preserved, is a state of raised risk [@rubino2025clinicalobesity].

The newer weight-loss medicines act on this circuit. **GLP-1 receptor agonists** (semaglutide, and
tirzepatide, a dual GIP/GLP-1 receptor agonist) are engineered, long-acting drugs that activate the
receptor for GLP-1, the gut satiety hormone (see [Gut hormones: short-term hunger and satiety signals](#sec-gut-peptides)). They
amplify endogenous satiety signalling: they shift the arcuate nucleus toward POMC/CART (satiety)
activity and slow gastric emptying, so hunger falls and meals end sooner (the fourth state of the
[interactive](#sec-thermostat)).

The medicines are effective. In the main trials, alongside lifestyle support, mean weight loss was
around 15% with semaglutide over 68 weeks and about 21% with tirzepatide at the top dose over 72 weeks,
against 2 to 3% with placebo, counting everyone randomised whether or not they stayed on the drug
[@wilding2021step1; @jastreboff2022surmount1]. When the drug stops, the
weight comes back, because the defended range was opposed, never removed
[@wilding2022step1extension]. Regain on stopping shows that obesity is a
chronic, regulated condition and that regain is not a failure of effort. (The classification
and management of obesity, including where these medicines and surgery fit, are in the
[*Obesity & metabolic syndrome*](obesity-metabolic-syndrome.qmd) chapter.)

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: a patient lost 10 kg on a diet. A year later she is hungrier than before and regaining. Why is this the expected outcome?
After weight loss, three systems shift together toward regain. Leptin falls disproportionately, so
the hypothalamus responds as it would to starvation; ghrelin rises and the satiety peptides fall,
changes that persist a year later; and energy expenditure falls more than predicted for the smaller body
(adaptive thermogenesis, or metabolic adaptation). Her regain is the predicted result of body-weight
regulation, not a failure of willpower.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: weight returns when a GLP-1 receptor agonist is stopped. What does that show about obesity?
The drug amplifies endogenous satiety signalling, shifting the arcuate nucleus toward POMC/CART
(satiety) activity and slowing gastric emptying. It opposes the defended range without removing it,
so when the drug stops the regulatory responses return and the weight comes back. Obesity therefore
behaves as a chronic, regulated condition, and regain after stopping is not a failure of effort.
:::

## Is it really just willpower? {#sec-close}

Willpower alone does not explain body weight, because appetite is a biologically regulated drive. The person who regains weight after a diet, who cannot
stop snacking on night shift, or who feels hungrier the more they diet is not weak: they are experiencing the expected result of their physiology.
Non-stigmatising medicine starts from that understanding. Energy balance (see the *Energy balance*
chapter) still applies, but it is biologically regulated rather than freely chosen.

## The Singapore context {#sec-singapore}

Singapore is a clear illustration of an **obesogenic food environment**: one in which palatable,
energy-dense food is cheap, abundant and always in view. That environment works together with the biology of
weight regulation, which is why the national "eat less, move more" message, while not wrong, is
insufficient. Adult obesity has risen in recent years, from 10.5% in 2019–2020 to 12.7% in 2023–2024
[@mohNPHS2024], despite sustained public-health effort, as would be expected of a regulated, environment-driven
system.

**The food environment encourages reward-driven eating.** Hawker centres, food courts and 24-hour options put
such food within reach day and night, and eating out is routine: in the 2010 National Nutrition Survey,
about 60% of Singaporeans ate out at least four times a week [@tan2020whereweeat].
Large refined-carbohydrate portions and sweet drinks are the easy default, and they engage the reward and cue responses (see
[Eating for pleasure](#sec-hedonic)).

**Nutri-Grade changes the environment instead of blaming the eater.** Sugary drinks are Singapore's
biggest source of dietary sugar. The Nutri-Grade scheme (A–D grades, plus an advertising ban on the
worst) is a concrete environmental measure targeting them, and industry responded even before it took effect: as
manufacturers reformulated ahead of the rules, the median sugar content of pre-packed graded drinks fell
from 7.1% in 2017 to 4.6% in 2021 [@mohNutriGradeRollout2022].

**Short sleep, exam stress and shift-work stress are common.** In a large multi-ethnic local cohort,
shorter and poorer sleep was associated with greater adiposity [@helios2024sleepadiposity], consistent with
the sleep experiments in [Sleep and stress](#sec-sleep-stress).

**The framing matters clinically.** Weight bias is common among Singapore's own healthcare
professionals [@goff2023weightbiassg], so understanding weight as a biologically regulated,
environmentally cued system is the basis for treating patients without blame.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Is "eat less, move more" enough?
The message rests on a real fact: a sustained energy deficit is still how weight is lost. It is
insufficient on its own, because it treats appetite and expenditure as freely chosen, whereas
both are biologically regulated and environmentally cued. When you discuss weight with a patient, the
useful approach is to change the environment and habits instead of relying on willpower against their
own physiology. The changes that help are the food kept at home, portion sizes, sleep, protein and fibre,
and eating more slowly. For some patients the regulatory responses are strong enough that medication or
specialist help is appropriate, and needing it is not a moral failing.
:::
